newsitem.title: HUNGARY: INVESTMENTS SEEN PUSHING HUNGARY 1997 GDP RISE - BB.
newsitem.headline: INVESTMENTS SEEN PUSHING HUNGARY 1997 GDP RISE - BB.

text.p: Economic growth in Hungary will pick up in 1997 on the back of investment expansion and a recovery in consumption, GE 's Hungarian bank unit, Budapest Bank said in its forecast.

Budapest Bank, one of the country's largest commercial banks, said it expected gross domestic product (GDP) to rise by one to three percentage points, Peter Bihari, head of the bank's economic analysis division, told a news conference on Friday.
The bank's expectations compare to an around two percent growth forecast laid down in Hungary's 1997 budget plan.

"We believe a modest revival in the pace of growth can be expected in 1997," Bihari said. "If zero to 0.5 percent growth is likely for 1996 then we expect the growth rate to between one and three percent (for 1997)."
"This doesn't mean a radical change in growth...but means a more favourable outlook for 1997," Bihari said.
The summary of the bank's analysis sees GDP amounting to 8,000 to 8,100 billion forints in 1997 at current prices.
An economic upturn next year will be based on internal factors, unlike in earlier years when growth was export-driven, he said.
"I would like to mention two factors, the likely revival of pace of investments and the likely halt in the decline of household consumption," Bihari said.

"The revival in investments next year is an essential change over 1996," he said. After stagnation or a slight rise in this area in 1996, Budapest Bank expects a six to eight percentage point rise in investments in 1997, he said.
This forecast is more conservative than that of the draft budget which sees investments growing by 10 to 12 percent.

Budapest Bank did not expect Hungary's external equilibrium to improve further in 1997, because spending of the general budget and the corporate sector will rise at a rate higher than household savings.
The bank expects Hungary's trade deficit to widen to $2.8 billion to $3.0 billion in 1997 from its estimate of $2.6 billion to $2.7 billion for 1996.
Rising investments as well as the phasing out of the current six percent import surcharge will result in rising imports, it added.
Meanwhile, the current account deficit is seen widening to $2.0 billion to $2.3 billion from Budapest Bank's estimate of $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion for this year.

The government forecasts a 1997 current account of between $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion in 1997, the same as in 1996 and also expects the trade deficit to remain unchanged at a similar figure of between $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion.
Budapest Bank sees consumer prices (CPI) rising 19 to 21 percent in 1997 againts its 1996 forecast of 23.5 to 23.8 percent.
These figures compare to the government's CPI forecast of 17 to 19 percent in 1997 and 23 to 24 percent in 1996.
